mardin.title: The Story of Mardin
mardin.cardTitle: A city of stone and plain
mardin.cardBody: Stone houses terraced down a hillside, three centuries as an Artuqid capital, and Mesopotamia opening to the horizon.
mardin.intro: Mardin is built on the southern slope of a long rocky ridge overlooking the Mesopotamian plain, almost entirely from local pale limestone. Houses step down with the incline, each one placed to see the plain over the roof of the one below; now and then the street carries on beneath a house, through a vaulted passage. Above sits the castle on the crest of the rock, below the plain runs to the horizon, and the city is squeezed into the narrow band between them.

blocks.title: A crossroads of civilizations
blocks.body: From its name in Assyrian records to the kingdom of Osroene, from a Roman frontier fortress to an Artuqid capital, from the Aq Qoyunlu to the Ottomans, every era added a layer to this stone. Excavations at the castle above the city uncover Artuqid, Aq Qoyunlu and Ottoman layers stacked on one another.

blocks.title: Stone terraced to the slope
blocks.body: Houses step down to follow the incline, are built around inner courtyards, and set their upper floors back from the courtyard. Vaulted abbara passages carry the street beneath the houses. UNESCO's tentative list assessment rests on exactly this terraced fabric and local stone architecture, calling the city the best preserved example of its kind.

blocks.title: Three centuries as an Artuqid capital
blocks.body: From 1103 the city was capital to one of the two main branches of the Artuqid dynasty. The minaret inscription of the Great Mosque records 1176, the portal of the Zinciriye records 3 February 1385 to the day. Most of the architecture you see today is the work of those three centuries.

blocks.title: Eight centuries of patriarchate
blocks.body: Deyrulzafaran, five kilometres east of the city, was founded in 493 and served for roughly eight centuries as the seat of the Syriac Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch. Inside the city, the Kirklar Church became the patriarchal church in 1293. The patriarchal seat ended in 1924 with the exile of the patriarch.

blocks.title: The sound of the bazaar
blocks.body: Coppersmiths' hammers still ring under the arcades. Traditional crafts recorded in the region include coppersmithing, filigree silver, stone carving, woodcarving and saddlery. Ottoman records count 74 shops in the Kayseriye Bazaar north of the Great Mosque in 1526, and 111 by 1564.

blocks.title: The architect of the last century
blocks.body: The Mardin-born architect Sarkis Lole rebuilt the ruined minaret of the Sehidiye in 1916 and 1917. The building raised in 1889 as a cavalry barracks, today the Sakip Sabanci Mardin City Museum, also carries his signature.

mardin.antiquityTitle: The first trace in Assyrian records
mardin.antiquityBody: A Neo-Assyrian legal document mentions a road to Mardiane, commonly identified with modern Mardin. As Aramean settlement grew, the Akkadian name fell out of use and gave way to the name Mardin.

timeline.title: First trace in Assyrian records
timeline.body: A Neo-Assyrian legal document records a road to Mardiane, commonly identified with modern Mardin.

timeline.title: The kingdom of Osroene
timeline.body: The city belongs to the kingdom of Osroene, ruled by the Abgarid dynasty.

timeline.title: Marida on the Roman frontier
timeline.body: The name Mardin first appears in the 4th-century historian Ammianus Marcellinus. In the Roman period the city is known as Marida, from a Syriac root meaning fortress.

timeline.title: Deyrulzafaran is founded
timeline.body: A site that had been a Roman fort and a Byzantine stronghold is turned into a monastery by Mor Shlemun. The Sasanians will destroy and abandon it in 607.

timeline.title: Rome builds a city on the plain
timeline.body: Emperor Anastasius I founds Dara as a frontier base against the Persians. Justinian's engineers later divert the Cordes river into the city by canal and build one of the earliest known arch dams to hold back its floods.

timeline.title: The Church of Mor Behnam
timeline.body: The church known today as Kirklar is built; Turkish sources give the year 569. In 1293 it will become the Syriac patriarchal church.

timeline.title: The coming of Islam
timeline.body: The Byzantine city is taken by the commander Iyad ibn Ghanm; heavy Arab settlement of the region begins and the city falls under the governorate of al-Jazira.

timeline.title: The monastery is reborn
timeline.body: Metropolitan Mor Hananyo buys and restores the ruined site, founds a manuscript library and grows the community to about eighty monks. The monastery has carried his name ever since.

timeline.title: The castle on the crest
timeline.body: The castle is most likely built under the Hamdanids; Hamdan ibn Hamdun takes it in 885 and the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tadid recovers it in 894.

timeline.title: An Artuqid capital
timeline.body: The city becomes capital to one of the two main branches of the Oghuz Turkish Artuqid dynasty, and over roughly three centuries reaches its architectural peak.

timeline.title: The inscription of the Great Mosque
timeline.body: The minaret inscription attributes the mosque to the Artuqid ruler Qutb al-Din Ilghazi II. Of the Artuqid building only the north wall and the carved wooden minbar survive.

timeline.title: A mihrab on the plain
timeline.body: The mosque begun at Dunaysir is completed under Abu'l Fath Artuq Arslan. Its mihrab carving is considered the summit of Artuqid stonework.

timeline.title: The Latifiye Mosque
timeline.body: Built by Abdullatif ibn Abdullah, who served under the Artuqid sultans Malik Salih and Malik Muzaffar, the mosque gives its name to the quarter around it.

timeline.title: The Zinciriye Medrese
timeline.body: The foundation inscription over the portal of the Sultan Isa Medrese records the completion date to the day. Sultan Isa was killed in battle and never buried in its tomb chamber.

timeline.title: Timur's second assault
timeline.body: Timur destroys the monastery's walls, cells and gate. The Great Mosque is also damaged in these invasions and loses its minaret.

timeline.title: Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu
timeline.body: The last Artuqid ruler yields the city to Qara Yusuf in 1409; the castle surrenders to the Aq Qoyunlu in 1432 and the rest of the century passes under their rule.

timeline.title: The Kasimiye is finished
timeline.body: Left unfinished when Sultan Isa was killed in 1407, the medrese is completed in the Aq Qoyunlu period in the name of Kasim, son of sultan Muizz al-Din. The water channel in its courtyard traces the course of a life from spring to pool.

timeline.title: The bazaar is built
timeline.body: The Kayseriye Bazaar north of the Great Mosque is thought to have been built in these years. Ottoman records count 74 shops in 1526, 80 in 1540 and 111 in 1564.

timeline.title: The Ottoman era
timeline.body: The town submits to the Ottomans in 1515 but the castle holds out; after Biyikli Mehmed Pasha returns with reinforcements the castle is taken in 1517.

timeline.title: The monastery press
timeline.body: The printing press bought from England in 1874 and installed at the monastery in 1881 produces its first book; a copy is sent to Queen Victoria.

timeline.title: The mansion on the square
timeline.body: Patriarch Ignatius Behnam Banni has the building raised as the Syriac Catholic Patriarchate. The same mansion will open as the Mardin Museum in 2000.

timeline.title: The minaret of the Sehidiye
timeline.body: The ruined minaret is rebuilt by the Mardin-born architect Sarkis Lole. With its floral carving and sun relief it is the most photographed minaret in the city.

timeline.title: UNESCO Tentative List
timeline.body: Mardin Cultural Landscape is submitted to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 25 February 2000. The listing covers both the city and Deyrulzafaran Monastery. Mardin is on the tentative list, not the World Heritage List.

nusaybin.title: The Story of Nusaybin
nusaybin.cardBody: A church and a mosque rising side by side, a mosaic thousands of years in the making.
nusaybin.intro: Nusaybin, known in antiquity as Nisibis, has lived for millennia on the fertile lands of Mesopotamia, along the Silk Road.

blocks.title: A crossroads of civilizations
blocks.body: From Assyrian to Roman, Persian to Syriac, Islamic to modern, every civilization left a layer and a story on this land.

blocks.title: A church and a mosque, side by side
blocks.body: In the heart of the city, the Mor Yakup Church and the Zeynel Abidin Mosque rise just a hundred metres apart. Centuries of coexistence among different faiths form Nusaybin's most striking symbol; both were added together to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2014.

blocks.title: A cradle of learning: the School of Nisibis
blocks.body: Ancient Nisibis was renowned for its school of theology and science, remembered as a cradle of learning.

nusaybin.antiquityBody: The city's name appears in Assyrian records as Nasibina as early as 901 BCE, giving Nusaybin nearly three thousand years of written history and making it one of Mesopotamia's most ancient settlements.

timeline.title: First named in Assyrian records
timeline.body: The city enters Assyrian inscriptions as the Aramean town of Nasibina and is soon annexed by the Assyrian Empire.

timeline.title: Alexander and the Hellenistic age
timeline.body: After Alexander the Great's conquest, the Seleucids re-found the city as Antiochia Mygdonia.

timeline.title: Three great sieges
timeline.body: On the Roman and Persian frontier, the Sasanian king Shapur II besieges the city three times, yet its walls hold; Nisibis is hailed as the Shield of the East.

timeline.title: Church of Mor Yakup
timeline.body: The Mor Yakup baptistery, the most important structure surviving from the ancient city, is built in this period. An Ancient Greek inscription on its middle frieze dates the work to the time of metropolitan Volagesus.

timeline.title: Rise of the School of Nisibis
timeline.body: The city's famous school becomes one of the foremost centres of theology and learning of its age.

timeline.title: The coming of Islam
timeline.body: The city peacefully joins the Islamic world under Caliph Umar and serves as an administrative centre.

timeline.title: The Zengid era
timeline.body: Under Nur al-Din Zengi the city is reshaped; an inscription dates the complex to 1159, raised on the site of a church dedicated to Saint Febronia of Nisibis.

timeline.title: The Ottoman era
timeline.body: Under Sultan Selim I, Nusaybin becomes part of the Ottoman Empire.

timeline.title: A district of Mardin
timeline.body: Today Nusaybin is a district of Mardin, carrying the legacy and multicultural fabric of ancient Nisibis.
